def: The single plant species all true tea comes from. White, green, yellow, oolong, black, and pu-erh are all made from its leaves — the difference is entirely in processing, not the plant.
also: Two main varieties are used commercially: sinensis (smaller leaf, cold-tolerant, common in China and Japan) and assamica (larger leaf, tropical, common in India and Yunnan).

def: The enzymatic browning reaction that occurs when tea leaf cells are broken and exposed to oxygen — the same process that turns a cut apple brown. Oxidation level is the primary thing separating tea categories from one another.
also: Frequently mislabeled as 'fermentation' on packaging, but true microbial fermentation only happens in pu-erh and other dark teas.

def: Applying heat to deactivate the enzymes responsible for oxidation, locking the leaf at its current state. Chinese greens are typically pan-fired; Japanese greens are typically steamed, which is why they taste noticeably different.
also: Known as shāqīng in Chinese.

def: Letting freshly plucked leaves lose moisture, making them pliable enough to roll without shattering. Length and conditions of the wither influence the final aroma.
also: White tea is essentially withering and drying with no other major step.

def: Shaping and bruising the leaf to break cell walls and start oxidation. Also determines the leaf's final visual form — twisted, balled, or flat.
Traditional tea production where whole leaves are kept largely intact through withering, rolling, oxidation, and drying. Produces more nuanced, complex teas than machine-driven methods.
also: Contrast with CTC.

def: An industrial method that runs leaves through toothed rollers, producing uniform granular pellets. Brews fast, strong, and dark — the standard for tea bags and blending.
also: Dominant in Assam, Kenya, and most bulk-production regions.

def: A single harvest period. Darjeeling famously has distinct first, second, monsoon, and autumn flushes, each producing a noticeably different cup from the same bushes.
also: First flush is typically lighter and more floral; second flush develops the muscatel character.

def: The season's earliest picking, after winter dormancy. Generally the most delicate and prized harvest, with concentrated flavor from slow winter growth.

A distinctive grape-like, slightly wine-adjacent flavor most associated with second-flush Darjeeling. Linked to leaves affected by a small insect (the tea jassid), whose feeding triggers a defensive response in the plant that alters flavor compounds.
The brewed tea itself — the liquid in the cup, as opposed to the dry leaf. Tasters assess its color, clarity, body, and aroma.
also: Nothing to do with alcohol.

def: The drying, mouth-puckering sensation from polyphenols binding to proteins in saliva. A normal, often desirable component of tea — distinct from bitterness, though the two often appear together.
also: Over-steeping or water that's too hot increases both.

def: The savory, brothy quality prominent in shaded Japanese greens like gyokuro and matcha. Comes largely from L-theanine and other amino acids, which shading preserves.
A Chinese tasting term for the returning sweetness felt in the throat after swallowing, especially valued in pu-erh and oolong. Literally 'returning sweet.'

A Chinese term for the physical or energetic sensation some drinkers report from certain teas, particularly aged pu-erh. Subjective and not scientifically defined, but widely discussed in tea circles.
A brewing approach using a high leaf-to-water ratio in a small vessel with many very short steeps, rather than one long steep. Reveals how a tea evolves across infusions.
also: Literally 'with skill' — the same gongfu as in kung fu.

def: A lidded bowl (typically 100–150ml) used for gongfu brewing. The lid strains leaves while pouring and can be used to smell the developing aroma.
also: Porcelain is the versatile default since it doesn't retain flavor between teas.

def: An unglazed clay teapot from Yixing, China. The porous clay absorbs tea oils over time, seasoning the pot — which is why they're traditionally dedicated to a single tea type.
The wide bowl used to whisk and drink matcha. Its width accommodates the whisk's motion.
The bamboo whisk used to prepare matcha, carved from a single piece of bamboo into dozens or over a hundred fine tines.
A small serving pitcher that brewed tea is decanted into before pouring into cups, so everyone gets equal strength rather than the first cup being weaker than the last.
The shade-grown, steamed, de-stemmed leaf that is ground into matcha. Matcha cannot legitimately be made from anything else — powdered sencha is a different (and lesser) product.
also: Tencha supply shortages since late 2024 are the root of current matcha authenticity problems.

def: Finely stone-ground tencha, whisked into water rather than steeped and strained — meaning you consume the whole leaf.
also: Ceremonial grade is meant for drinking straight; culinary grade is formulated for baking and lattes.

def: A Japanese green tea shaded for several weeks before harvest, producing intense umami and sweetness with reduced astringency.
also: Brewed much cooler than most teas — often 50–60°C.

def: Japan's most common green tea: steamed, rolled into needles, and grown in full sun. Grassy, brisk, and marine in character.
Japanese green tea roasted over charcoal or in a pan until brown. Roasting drives off much of the caffeine and astringency, giving a toasty, mellow cup.
also: Often served in the evening or to children in Japan for this reason.

def: Green tea blended with roasted brown rice, some of which pops like popcorn. Nutty and comforting, and historically a way to stretch expensive tea.
Pu-erh that is sun-dried and compressed without the accelerated wet-piling step, then aged naturally over years or decades. Starts bright and astringent, mellowing dramatically with age.
Pu-erh put through a controlled 'wet piling' (wo dui) fermentation that simulates decades of aging in a matter of weeks. Earthy, smooth, and ready to drink immediately.
also: Developed in the 1970s to meet demand for aged character without the wait.

def: The controlled microbial fermentation used to make ripe pu-erh, where damp leaf is heaped and turned under monitored humidity and temperature for weeks.
The loose, sun-dried base material that pu-erh is made from before compression or fermentation. Can be drunk as-is or set aside for aging.
Tea compressed into a round disc, the most common format for pu-erh. Compression slows and shapes how the tea ages.
also: Standard sizes are often 357g.

def: Oolongs grown in the mineral-rich, rocky terrain of the Wuyi Mountains. Known for a distinctive mineral quality tasters call 'rock rhyme' (yan yun).
also: Da Hong Pao is the most famous example.

def: Phoenix Mountain oolongs from individual old tea bushes, famed for naturally mimicking specific fruit and flower aromas — honey orchid, almond, gardenia — without any added flavoring.
also: Literally 'single bush.'

def: Taiwanese oolong grown above roughly 1,000m. Cooler temperatures and mist slow growth, concentrating flavor and producing a characteristically creamy, floral cup.
An amino acid abundant in tea, associated with a calm-but-alert state. Often credited for why tea's caffeine feels different from coffee's.
also: Shading (as with gyokuro and matcha) increases its concentration.

def: The main class of polyphenols in tea and the source of much of its astringency and antioxidant activity. EGCG is the most-studied one, and is highest in less-oxidized teas.
The combined effect of altitude, soil, climate, and local growing conditions on a tea's character — the reason the same cultivar tastes different in Darjeeling than in Nepal.
also: Borrowed from wine.

def: A specific cultivated variety of the tea plant, selected for traits like cold-hardiness, flavor, or yield. Yabukita dominates Japan; Taiwan's Ruby #18 and Qing Xin are widely planted.
Chinese green tea picked before the Qingming festival in early April. Highly prized and priced accordingly, since the pre-festival window is short and yields are small.
also: Also written 'Ming Qian.'
